name: Samsung-cl
title: CL series multilayer ceramic chip capacitors, commercial and industrial

source.document: Multilayer ceramic capacitors, Part Ⅰ Commercial/Industrial

summary: The CL series is a range of surface-mount multilayer ceramic chip capacitors from 008004 (0201 metric) to 2220 (5750 metric), in class Ⅰ (C0G, X8G) and class Ⅱ (X5R, X6S, X6T, X7R, X7S, X7T, Y5V, X8M, X8L, JIS-B) dielectrics, rated from 2.5 V to 3 kV. Each part number spells out size, dielectric, capacitance, tolerance, voltage, thickness, construction, reliability grade and packing. Besides standard chips there are industrial High Level Ⅰ and Ⅱ grades and special molded-frame, land-side, soft-termination, low-noise and low-ESL builds.

operation.text: The CL family spans plain chip capacitors at three reliability grades (Standard, High Level Ⅰ, High Level Ⅱ) and special builds: molded frame (MFC), land side (LSC) for mounting between solder balls in thin devices and modules, high bending strength with soft metal-epoxy terminations, low acoustic noise (THMC and ANSC types), and low ESL (reverse geometry, 3T and 8T).
A ceramic body holds Ni inner electrodes (Cu in some parts); terminations are Cu or Cu with metal epoxy, plated first with Ni and then Sn. MFC parts add a frame and epoxy molding compound.

Standard parts suit phones, TVs, PCs and consumer power; High Level Ⅰ adds moisture margin (65 ℃, 90 %RH, 500 h) for servers, networks and industrial power; High Level Ⅱ is tested at 85 ℃, 85 %RH for 1000 h and 1000 temperature cycles for outdoor industrial use such as base stations and solar inverters. Positions 9 and 10 of the part number name the grade.

Class Ⅱ ceramic flexes under AC or pulsed voltage by the piezoelectric effect and can make the board hum in the 20 Hz to 20 kHz band. The low-noise types fit the same footprint as the parts they replace.

Class Ⅱ capacitance moves with applied AC and DC voltage, so the measurement level matters; a meter with auto level control should hold the set voltage, and at high capacitance or frequency it can fall short of it.
Loss is given as Q for class Ⅰ parts, whose DF is very small, and as DF for class Ⅱ parts. Class Ⅰ parts suit coupling, filters and timing where low loss and linearity count.
Leakage under DC is small; charging current dies away over time, so insulation resistance is read one minute after rated voltage is applied.
Class Ⅱ capacitance falls roughly linearly with the logarithm of time; class Ⅰ does not age. One hour at 150 ℃ restores the lost capacitance and restarts the aging clock.
AC or pulse current through the ESR heats the part. Its surface, self-heating included, must stay within the maximum operating temperature, and the rise from self-heating must stay at or below 20 ℃.

Below the self-resonant frequency the part is capacitive and ESR comes mostly from dielectric loss; above it the part is inductive (ESL) and ESR comes mostly from the electrode metal. At resonance only ESR remains. A network analyzer's small test signal can read low capacitance because of the AC voltage dependence.

Parts life-tested at only 100 % of rated voltage are marked derated; to match the life of a part tested at 150 %, their voltage is reduced with temperature: full rated voltage up to 20 ℃ below the maximum temperature, falling to 70 % at the maximum, measured as surface temperature with self-heating.

DC, or the peak of DC plus AC, must not exceed rated voltage; for pure AC or pulses the peak-to-peak value must not exceed it; surges and static must not exceed it either. Surge current can overshoot the capacitor voltage past the surge itself, and ESD stresses low-value parts most.

Orient the long axis of the chip parallel to the direction of board bending stress; keep parts away from board cut lines and screw holes; support the board under the placement head and test probes; bending, twisting, depaneling, dropping, lead insertion, connectors and screw tightening can all crack the chip, and a cracked part can short.

Preheat the board and part to keep the temperature difference small, keep the reflow peak at 240 to 260 °C and fewer than three reflows, cool in air, and size the land and paste so the solder fillet is neither too high (cracking) nor too thin (weak joint). Sn-Zn solder lowers reliability.

Use flux at 0.1 % halogen or less, applied thin; rosin flux needs no cleaning; strong ultrasonic or pressure cleaning can crack joints. Adhesive and coating resin should be insulating, low-shrink and close to the chip's thermal expansion; silicone under-coat buffers stress, and hygroscopic or acidic resins degrade insulation.
A cracked or overstressed capacitor can fail short; a fuse or similar protection belongs in circuits where that short could cause further harm.
Store at 0 to 40 °C and 0 to 70 %RH without corrosive gas, and use within six months. In service avoid water, oil, direct sunlight, ozone, UV, corrosive gas, excess vibration and high humidity.
